Asylum seekers win ruling against home secretary’s reduction of safeguards for potential victims of trafficking The British home secretary’s decision to reduce protections for potential trafficking victims to allow the “one in, one out” asylum returns deal to proceed was unlawful, a high court judge has ruled. The legal challenge was brought by five small boat asylum seekers earmarked for return to France – four from Eritrea and one from Sudan. It related to a change in guidance on the one in, one out scheme, which meant that those denied trafficking protections no longer had the right to ask for it to be reconsidered.

The judgment is likely to have significant implications, with many asylum seekers who arrive in small boats potentially victims of trafficking, especially if they have passed through Libya on their journey to the UK. The one in, one out deal involves one person who has travelled from France to the UK on a small boat being forcibly returned to France in exchange for another asylum seeker in France who has not attempted to cross the Channel. Mahmood amended the trafficking reconsideration guidance in order to expedite returns of some small boat arrivals to France. Since the scheme started last August it is likely that more than 1,000 people have been removed to France under the scheme. Many have subsequently disappeared. Hundreds more small boat arrivals are in UK detention centres awaiting forced return to France.

In a lengthy judgment published on Friday morning, Mr Justice Sheldon found that Shabana Mahmood’s decision on the guidance was unlawful, prompting lawyers for some of those affected to call for their clients to be returned to the UK. Other elements relating to individual decisions taken by the home secretary concerning the five cases were found to be lawful. The judge found that the decision to amend the trafficking guidance to prevent reconsideration of cases given an initial negative decision made a “real difference” in two of the asylum seekers’ cases, but did not make a difference in two of the other cases. All five asylum seekers were given permission by the judge to proceed with their legal claims.

Shabana Mahmood's move to make refugee status temporary will be challenged in the courts, The Independent can reveal.

Under sweeping changes to the asylum and immigration rules in March, home secretary Shabana Mahmood changed the amount of time a refugee can stay for in the UK, saying that her reforms offered "a compassionate but controlled asylum system".

Asylum seekers' cases will now be reviewed every 30 months, after which they could be sent back to their country of origin. Previously, refugees with successful asylum claims were given a five-year visa and could apply to stay in the UK indefinitely after the five-years.

Now charity Asylum Aid has launched legal action against the Home Office over the decision to cut the grant of refugee leave from five years to two and a half.

Asylum Aid will argue that the changes are unlawful and will cause serious harm by increasing instability and undermining refugees' integration into the UK.

The charity has sent a pre-action letter to the government that says that the home secretary failed to adequately assess the impact of her policy change on refugees, including on children and other vulnerable groups.

payload.title: Britannian korkea oikeus kumosi ihmiskaupan uhrien suojaa heikentäneen ohjemuutoksen
payload.summary: Britannian korkea oikeus katsoi sisäministeri Shabana Mahmoodin tekemän ohjemuutoksen lainvastaiseksi. Muutos esti kielteisen ihmiskauppapäätöksen saaneita turvapaikanhakijoita pyytämästä asian uudelleenarviointia.
payload.content:
Britannian korkean oikeuden tuomari on katsonut lainvastaiseksi sisäministeri Shabana Mahmoodin päätöksen, jolla vähennettiin mahdollisten ihmiskaupan uhrien oikeusturvaa. Ohjemuutoksen tarkoituksena oli nopeuttaa turvapaikanhakijoiden palautuksia Britannian ja Ranskan välisen niin sanotun yksi sisään, yksi ulos -järjestelyn nojalla.

## Viisi turvapaikanhakijaa haastoi muutoksen

Oikeudellisen haasteen nosti viisi pienellä veneellä Britanniaan saapunutta turvapaikanhakijaa, jotka oli määrä palauttaa Ranskaan. Heistä neljä on Eritreasta ja yksi Sudanista. Kiista koski ohjeistusta, jota sovelletaan mahdollisiin ihmiskaupan uhreihin. Muutoksen jälkeen ensimmäisessä käsittelyssä kielteisen päätöksen saanut hakija ei enää voinut pyytää ihmiskauppaan liittyvän suojelutarpeensa uudelleenarviointia.

Tuomari Sheldon totesi perjantaiaamuna julkaistussa laajassa ratkaisussa, että Mahmoodin päätös muuttaa ohjeistusta oli lainvastainen. Tuomarin mukaan uudelleenarvioinnin estäminen vaikutti tosiasiallisesti kahden kantajan tilanteeseen, mutta kahdessa muussa tapauksessa muutos ei vaikuttanut lopputulokseen. Ratkaisussa ei kerrottu vastaavasta vaikutuksesta viidennen kantajan osalta.

Kaikki viisi turvapaikanhakijaa saivat luvan jatkaa oikeudellisia vaatimuksiaan. Tuomioistuin piti kuitenkin lainmukaisina muita sisäministerin tekemiä, kantajien yksittäisiä tapauksia koskevia ratkaisuja. Joidenkin asianosaisten asianajajat vaativat tuomion jälkeen, että heidän Ranskaan palautetut asiakkaansa tuotaisiin takaisin Britanniaan.

## Päätös voi vaikuttaa palautusjärjestelyyn

Britannian ja Ranskan järjestelyssä pienellä veneellä Ranskasta Britanniaan matkustanut henkilö voidaan palauttaa pakolla Ranskaan. Vastineeksi Britannia ottaa vastaan Ranskassa olevan turvapaikanhakijan, joka ei ole yrittänyt ylittää Englannin kanaalia. Mahmood muutti ihmiskauppapäätösten uudelleenarviointia koskevaa ohjeistusta nopeuttaakseen joidenkin veneillä saapuneiden palautuksia.

Järjestelyn käynnistyttyä viime elokuussa Ranskaan on lähdeaineiston mukaan todennäköisesti palautettu yli tuhat ihmistä, ja monet heistä ovat sittemmin kadonneet viranomaisten seurannasta. Lisäksi Britannian säilöönottokeskuksissa on satoja pienillä veneillä saapuneita odottamassa mahdollista pakkopalautusta. Ratkaisulla voi olla laajoja seurauksia, koska monet meritse saapuvat voivat olla ihmiskaupan uhreja, erityisesti jos heidän matkansa Britanniaan on kulkenut Libyan kautta.
summary_bullets: Korkea oikeus katsoi ihmiskauppasuojelua koskeneen ohjemuutoksen lainvastaiseksi.
Kanteen nosti viisi Ranskaan palautettavaksi määrättyä turvapaikanhakijaa.
Päätös voi vaikuttaa yli tuhanteen jo tehtyyn palautukseen sekä satoihin säilöönotettuina odottaviin hakijoihin.
payload.journalist_note: Ratkaisun ydinkohdat ja palautusjärjestelyn toimintaperiaate käyvät lähdeaineistosta selvästi ilmi. Palautettujen määrä on lähteessä arvio, joten se on ilmaistu varauksellisesti.

Asylum seekers win ruling against home secretary’s reduction of safeguards for potential victims of trafficking The British home secretary’s decision to reduce protections for potential trafficking victims to allow the “one in, one out” asylum returns deal to proceed was unlawful, a high court judge has ruled. The legal challenge was brought by five small boat asylum seekers earmarked for return to France – four from Eritrea and one from Sudan. It related to a change in guidance on the one in, one out scheme, which meant that those denied trafficking protections no longer had the right to ask for it to be reconsidered.

The judgment is likely to have significant implications, with many asylum seekers who arrive in small boats potentially victims of trafficking, especially if they have passed through Libya on their journey to the UK. The one in, one out deal involves one person who has travelled from France to the UK on a small boat being forcibly returned to France in exchange for another asylum seeker in France who has not attempted to cross the Channel. Mahmood amended the trafficking reconsideration guidance in order to expedite returns of some small boat arrivals to France. Since the scheme started last August it is likely that more than 1,000 people have been removed to France under the scheme. Many have subsequently disappeared. Hundreds more small boat arrivals are in UK detention centres awaiting forced return to France.

In a lengthy judgment published on Friday morning, Mr Justice Sheldon found that Shabana Mahmood’s decision on the guidance was unlawful, prompting lawyers for some of those affected to call for their clients to be returned to the UK. Other elements relating to individual decisions taken by the home secretary concerning the five cases were found to be lawful. The judge found that the decision to amend the trafficking guidance to prevent reconsideration of cases given an initial negative decision made a “real difference” in two of the asylum seekers’ cases, but did not make a difference in two of the other cases. All five asylum seekers were given permission by the judge to proceed with their legal claims.
